Telecommunications Spaces: TR, ER, EF, and TE

Unit 3: Pathways and Spaces. Lesson 11 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

The foreman points at a janitor closet and says that is the new TR. Water pipes cross the ceiling and a floor drain sits in the middle. The room has to be right before the first rack goes in, because every cable on the floor ends here.

What each space serves

A TR serves one floor or part of one. An ER serves the whole building or campus and houses large equipment. An EF is where outside cabling enters the building. A TE is a cabinet that serves a small zone of at most 335 square meters (3600 square feet) on a floor. A TE is never a substitute for a TR.

Location

  • At least one TR per floor, on the same floor as the work areas it serves.
  • Place it so that no horizontal cable run passes 90 m.
  • Stack TRs vertically so backbone pathways run straight.

Environment

The room needs conditioned air, clean and dry conditions, good lighting, power outlets on dedicated, nonswitched circuits, and bonding already in place. The floor must carry the load of full racks, so ask the designer. The door must lock and be wide enough to move equipment in.

Do not put in a TR: water pipes or drains over the equipment, unrelated equipment, storage, or anything that blocks the door.

The backboard

Item          Rule
Material      plywood, void free, A grade exposed, C grade on the wall, 15 percent moisture or less
Thickness     19 mm (3/4 in); sheets 1.2 m by 2.4 m (4 ft by 8 ft)
Height        from 203 mm (8 in) above the floor to 2.6 m (8.5 ft)
Paint         two coats of fire-retardant paint; if fire-retardant treated, do not paint
Where         at least two walls; all four if possible
Fasteners     on studs, screws 12.7 mm (0.5 in) longer than the plywood is thick

If no clearance distance is specified, plan at least 1 m (3.28 ft) around and between equipment.

Tip: lay out the backboard on the drawing and mark the conduit entries before the plywood goes up.
Exam tip: a TE serves at most 335 square meters, and it never replaces a TR. A TR needs at least one per floor.
Remember
A TR serves a floor, an ER the building, an EF the outside world, and a TE a small zone; keep water out and the backboard void free.
Deeper explanation

Telecommunications Spaces: TR, ER, EF, and TE, explained slowly

Does the TR reach the far corner?

The reach rule says that no horizontal cable run may pass 90 m. A TR placed badly on a long floor can leave outlets out of range. Check the room against the farthest outlet on the floor before the walls go up.

Option                           Route to farthest outlet   Result
TR at the east end               77 m + 8 m drop and slack  85 m  passes
TR at the west end               88 m + 8 m drop and slack  96 m  fails
TR in the center core            45 m + 8 m drop and slack  53 m  passes

The drop and slack allowance is real cable. It is easy to forget when you scale the plan.

A checklist for a new TR

Check                 What you look for
Location              same floor as the work areas; centered in the core when possible
Reach                 no run over 90 m
Stacking              rooms line up from floor to floor for the backbone
Environment           conditioned air, clean, dry, lit well enough to read a label
Power                 dedicated, nonswitched duplex outlets
Bonding               a busbar installed and the TBB reachable
Door                  lockable, wide enough to move equipment
Floor load            checked with the designer for full racks
Intruders             no water pipes over the equipment, no storage

Backboard layout, worked

A TR has two walls plywood-covered. Each sheet is 1.2 m by 2.4 m (4 ft by 8 ft). A wall that is 3.6 m (11.8 ft) long needs 3.6 / 1.2 = 3 sheets set on edge, which means the 2.4 m dimension runs vertical. The plywood runs from 203 mm (8 in) above the floor to 2.6 m (8.5 ft). Do not split the difference in a taller room. Paint it with two coats of fire-retardant paint, unless the code requires fire-retardant treated plywood, in which case you do not paint it and you ask the AHJ whether the stamp stays visible.

Fastening

On wood studs, align the sheet to the studs. On metal studs, use screws at least 12.7 mm (0.5 in) longer than the plywood is thick. In a hollow wall, use toggle bolts at least 6.3 mm (0.25 in) in diameter, 51 mm (2 in) from the edges and about every 610 mm (24 in). Leave no gaps between sheets.

The TE

A TE serves at most 335 square meters (3600 square feet) on a floor and never replaces a TR. A metal TE is bonded.

Remember: reach first, then environment, then backboard.
